title: Approve a safe, effective and reversible hormonal male contraceptive

concept.text: Prevent pregnancy through reversible hormonal suppression of sperm production while maintaining androgen-dependent functions. NES/testosterone gel has completed phase 2b evaluation in couples; approval remains outstanding. Proposed completion test: FDA approval after a pivotal couples study with at least 500 couple-years of contraceptive exposure, a pregnancy rate below 2 per 100 couple-years, acceptable safety, and documented recovery of sperm production and fertility after cessation. Test set by: FDA would decide approval; WHO's September 2026 male-contraceptive TPP establishes efficacy, safety and reversibility as development criteria. The exposure minimum and pregnancy-rate threshold here are editorial proposals. Sources given: [WHO male contraceptive target product profiles](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240124950) ; [NICHD 2025 contraceptive development report](https://annualreport.nichd.nih.gov/blithe.html) ; [Developer's current clinical pipeline](https://www.contraline.com/trials).

page.title: Reversible hormonal male contraception
page.definition: An approved hormonal drug for men prevents pregnancy by suppressing sperm production while maintaining testosterone-dependent functions, including sexual function. Sperm production recovers after treatment stops.

goal.need: In 2021, 164 million women aged 15–49 worldwide had an unmet need for contraception. Men's participation remains largely confined to condoms, vasectomy and withdrawal. The goal is an additional reversible drug-based contraceptive option for men.

statements.quote: To expand men's contraceptive choices, efforts are underway to develop safe, effective and reversible novel male contraceptive methods and delivery systems.
with the goal of obtaining FDA–regulatory approval.
statements.context: The Contraceptive Clinical Trials Network advances candidate contraceptive drugs and devices through clinical development.

completion.title: FDA approves a hormonal male contraceptive for reversible pregnancy prevention.
completion.criterion: FDA issues an approval letter for a new drug application for reversible hormonal male contraception. The product meets statutory standards for safety, effectiveness, manufacturing and controls, and labeling. Adequate clinical evidence supports its intended contraceptive use and claimed reversibility under the approved conditions of use.
completion.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.105(c) and 314.125(b).
completion.threshold_quote: FDA will approve an NDA after it determines that the drug meets the statutory standards for safety and effectiveness, manufacturing and controls, and labeling,
completion.basis: NICHD explicitly seeks FDA approval. The approval decision evaluates the intended use and the complete evidence package. WHO's target profiles guide development and regulatory review. Contraline identifies NES/T gel as investigational and unapproved.

milestones.title: Preclinical studies support human testing of a hormonal male contraceptive.
milestones.criterion: Animal or in-vitro pharmacology and toxicology support the conclusion that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe; applicable studies follow Good Laboratory Practice. A 2025 paper reported GLP oral toxicology of dimethandrolone undecanoate in cynomolgus macaques, with 6–7 males per group treated for 9 months and no significant toxicological findings.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8), governing the preclinical evidence supporting an investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: Phase 1 establishes human pharmacokinetics and tolerability of a hormonal male contraceptive.
milestones.criterion: Human studies establish drug absorption, disposition, pharmacological effects and dose-related adverse effects sufficiently to design phase 2 studies. In the 2019 oral dimethandrolone undecanoate phase 1b report, 100 men received study drug or placebo for 28 days; 83 completed treatment and 82 entered the efficacy-evaluable analysis. No serious adverse events occurred; body weight and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol showed dose effects.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), defining the information required from phase 1 investigations.
milestones.threshold_quote: sufficient information about the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacological effects should be obtained to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: A hormonal male contraceptive suppresses sperm concentration to ≤1 million/mL.
milestones.criterion: Couples begin sole-method use after sperm concentration reaches ≤1 million/mL. In 2012, a trial randomized 99 men to testosterone with nestorone or placebo gels; 56 adherent men treated for at least 20 weeks were analysed. Suppression occurred in 89% with 8 mg nestorone and 88% with 12 mg; median serum testosterone remained in the adult male range.
milestones.set_by: European Academy of Andrology and American Society of Andrology, recommendation 45.

milestones.title: Over 95% of men regain the adult sperm concentration range within 6 months of stopping hormonal contraception.
milestones.criterion: After stopping treatment, over 95% regain the adult sperm concentration range; assess recovery over 6 months in phase IIb/III. Recovery time depends on formulation. Sperm recovery is a surrogate for fertility. In a 2016 study enrolling 320 men, injectable norethisterone enanthate plus testosterone undecanoate produced estimated recovery of 94.8% at 52 weeks (95% CI 91.5–97.1). Recruitment and injections ended early following an external safety review.
milestones.set_by: European Academy of Andrology and American Society of Andrology, section 10.4, proposed regulatory recommendations.
milestones.threshold_quote: recovery after hormonal male contraception should be over 95%.

milestones.title: A hormonal male contraceptive reaches 5,000 men-months of couples efficacy exposure.
milestones.criterion: The societies propose 5,000 men-months, with a 365-day Kaplan–Meier pregnancy analysis during sole-method use. A 2009 phase III testosterone-undecanoate study enrolled 1,045 men; 855 entered efficacy follow-up, with 9 pregnancies over 1,554.1 person-years and a 24-month cumulative failure probability of 1.1%. On 4 February 2026, Contraline reported completion of NES/T phase 2b in 462 couples; that announcement supplies no numerical pregnancy endpoint and is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: European Academy of Andrology and American Society of Andrology, section 10.4; this is a proposed study-exposure target.
milestones.threshold_quote: 5000 men-months of exposure would be sufficient to demonstrate efficacy.

milestones.title: A hormonal male contraceptive has safety exposure in about 1,500 men, including 100 treated for one year.
milestones.criterion: For one product, the general ICH safety database comprises about 1,500 exposed individuals, usually including 300–600 treated for 6 months and 100 for at least 1 year at intended clinical doses. The andrology societies recommend at least 300 men for the 6-month component. ICH allows exceptions, including larger databases for preventive treatment of healthy people. Contraline's pipeline lists NES/T phase III planning.
milestones.set_by: International Conference on Harmonisation, E1A guideline adopted by FDA; applied to male contraception in EAA–ASA recommendation 44.
milestones.threshold_quote: 100 patients exposed for a minimum of one-year is considered to be acceptable to include as part of the safety data base.

not_found: The final WHO target-product-profile PDF published on 22 September 2026 could not be downloaded from WHO IRIS because access returned HTTP 403.
No male-specific FDA guidance specifying a universal pregnancy-rate cutoff or minimum couple-years of contraceptive exposure was found.
No peer-reviewed report of the completed NES/T phase 2b pregnancy and sperm-recovery endpoints was found.
No complete product-specific safety database documenting the recommended total and duration-specific exposures was located.

results.finding: Oral DMAU in cynomolgus macaques (6–7 males per group): no significant toxicological findings after 9 months.
results.detail: The oral toxicity study complied with FDA Good Laboratory Practice regulations. Its favorable safety profile supported initiation of a Phase 1 trial in men.
results.quote: Repeat dose oral and IM administrations were well‐tolerated with no significant toxicological findings.

results.finding: In a phase 1b trial, 100 men received oral DMAU or placebo; no serious adverse events occurred.
results.detail: After 28 days, 83 completed the study and 82 were efficacy-evaluable. The study characterized pharmacokinetics, hormone suppression, and dose effects on weight, HDL cholesterol and sexual desire, supporting further testing.
results.quote: Two hundred and two research participants were screened, 100 were randomized and received study medication, and 83 completed the study.

results.finding: In an injectable hormone trial of 320 men, 95.9 per 100 continuing users reached ≤1 million sperm/mL within 24 weeks.
results.detail: Couples were asked to rely solely on the injections after two qualifying semen samples. This was a single-arm injectable trial, not the specified randomized testosterone–nestorone gel trial.
results.quote:
Of the 320 participants, 95.9 of 100 continuing users (95% confidence interval [CI], 92.8 –
97.9) suppressed to a sperm concentration less than or equal to 1 million/mL within 24 weeks
(Kaplan-Meier method).

results.finding: Among 247 men in the recovery analysis, estimated sperm recovery was 94.8% by 52 weeks of recovery.
results.detail: The study reports recovery below 95% at 52 weeks of recovery, which began 8 weeks after the final injection; it does not establish the threshold within 6 months. Recovery was defined by sperm concentration or total count. The study was described as phase II, without a stated IIb designation.
results.quote:
The cumulative reversibility of suppression of spermatogenesis after 52 weeks
of recovery was 94.8 per 100 continuing users (95% CI, 91.5–97.1).

results.finding: Among 1,549 men, the typical probability of sperm recovery to 20 million/mL within 6 months was 67%.
results.detail: The estimate is below the required 95%. It pools 30 studies of androgen or androgen-progestagen regimens; the text does not specify their trial phases.
results.quote: The typical probability of recovery to 20 million per mL was 67% (61-72) within 6 months, 90% (85-93) within 12 months, 96% (92-98) within 16 months, and 100% within 24 months.
